reasons: Several failures are ignored silently, so errors may go unnoticed.
Some fields use loose typing shortcuts, which hides mistakes from the compiler.
Admin rights must be enforced on the server, which this file does not show.

sections.name: File setup, InviteCode
sections.title: Imports and invite record shape
sections.what: Brings in React tools, the navigation link, shared page pieces and the settings helpers. Defines what one invite code record holds: the code, whether it was used, who used it and when it was created.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed shape keeps the invite data the same between the server and this page.
sections.watch_out: If the server changes the invite fields, this shape must change too, or the list shows wrong data.

sections.name: SettingsPage (part 1)
sections.title: Page memory, loading and admin actions
sections.what: Keeps the chosen provider, keys, save flags, service settings, admin flag and invite list. On open it reloads saved choices and checks for admin rights. It also holds the actions that create an invite code, copy an invite link and save service settings, and it looks up the selected provider.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page must show what the user saved last time and show admin tools only to admins.
sections.watch_out: The admin check is a request that can fail. Failures are ignored, so the admin section simply stays hidden.

sections.name: SettingsPage (part 2)
sections.title: Saving the chosen AI model
sections.what: When the user saves, stores the chosen provider, its model name and the key for that provider, then shows a short saved message.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app needs to know which AI service and key to use for later requests.
sections.watch_out: The key is saved only when the provider needs one. Keys for other providers stay in page memory until the page closes.

sections.name: SettingsPage (part 3)
sections.title: Provider cards and key entry
sections.what: Draws one selectable card per AI provider, showing its price and description. The selected card reveals a masked box for that provider's key and a link to get a key.
sections.why: Likely reason: showing one key field at a time keeps the form simple.
sections.watch_out: Typed keys stay in page memory until the user saves them.

sections.name: SettingsPage (part 4)
sections.title: Service fields and sender identity
sections.what: Shows the optional services section: keys for contact discovery, email sending and email checking, plus a sender name and sender email used for sending.
sections.why: Likely reason: these services are optional, so each one gets its own key field.
sections.watch_out: The sender email must be a domain verified with the email service, or sending will fail.

sections.name: SettingsPage (part 5)
sections.title: Save buttons, data note and new code panel
sections.what: Holds the save button for service settings and the note that profile and application data stay in the browser. For admins it shows the generate button and, after generating, the new code with a copy link button.
sections.why: Likely reason: the note tells users their data is not on the server, and the new code is shown once so it can be copied.
sections.watch_out: The invite link is built from the current site address, so it points to whichever domain the admin is using.

sections.name: SettingsPage (part 6)
sections.title: Invite code list
sections.what: Lists every invite code with its status. Open codes get a copy link button. Used codes show who used them.
sections.why: Likely reason: the admin needs to see which codes are still free to hand out.
sections.watch_out: The used-by names come from server data, so they are only as accurate as that data.

summary: Settings page where the user picks an AI provider, enters API keys that stay in the browser, sets optional service keys, and lets an admin create and track invite codes.
purpose: Lets the user choose which AI model the app uses and keep their own keys, and lets the admin manage invitations.
why: Likely reason: keys are kept in the browser so the app does not need to store them on its servers.
how: 1. Loads the saved provider, keys and service settings from browser storage. 2. Asks `/api/auth/me` whether the current user is an admin. 3. If so, loads invite codes from `/api/admin/invite`. 4. The user picks a provider, enters its key and saves. 5. Service keys are saved the same way. 6. An admin can generate codes and copy invite links.
inputs: Clicks and typing on the page, saved settings in browser storage, the current user from `/api/auth/me`, and invite codes from `/api/admin/invite`.
outputs: Saved settings in browser storage, a new invite code for the admin, and invite links copied to the clipboard.
risks: API keys and service keys sit in browser storage, which scripts on the same site can read. The admin section is only hidden in this page, so the server must enforce admin rights on `/api/admin/invite` (not visible here). The page says keys are never stored on the server, but this file alone cannot prove that.
debug: If settings do not stick, check the browser's saved data for the app and the save functions in `lib/model-settings` and `lib/integration-settings`. If the admin section is missing, check the reply from `/api/auth/me`. If invite codes do not load, check the `/api/admin/invite` replies.
